cells.tense: The letting-go is happening now, at your pace, with the pen in your hand.
cells.act: make the fair call about a feeling, yourself
cells.ask: Name where the scale between you and someone actually sits — say it out loud, alone, no audience. Then let the feeling that follows run its course before you do anything about it.
cells.core:
You can tell what to keep and what to let go, and you tell it without running numbers. Something ends, the ground gets turned, and what comes next grows there because you let the ending be an ending instead of arguing it down. Folks near you get steadier when you do the deciding, and nobody has to announce it.

What's here now: your appetite is pointed at something real, not at a picture of wanting. That makes the fair call simpler — you're naming what's true between you and someone, not calculating, and leaving it said. The back-and-forth keeps moving when no one's keeping score. This time say the call out loud, even alone, where nothing repeats it back. A decision that's been spoken tends to hold.
cells.sheetLine: You know what to keep, and you let the rest finish.
cells.verb: Deciding what to release and what to keep, then standing behind the call
cells.place: the room where what you want pulls you forward before there's a route

cells.tense: You are bracing for an ending that hasn't come, and rehearsing it ahead of time.
cells.act: hold space for what someone feels without fixing it
cells.ask: Next time someone close is upset, don't improve the situation. Ask what it feels like and sit with whatever comes back. Stay until it's said, not until it's fixed.
cells.core:
You let go early. Something is still growing and you've already filed it as finished, or something is finished and you keep turning the soil anyway. Either way the timing comes from you rather than from the thing itself, and you're a step ahead of what's actually here, braced for an ending you wrote in your head.

The pull toward what you want runs strong, and that's the difficulty — it keeps outrunning what the day can hold, so you press the people near you toward a decision they haven't reached. What steadies it is staying inside someone's feeling instead of managing it. Not repairing, not steering them toward the ending you can already see. Given a week, most of what you're preparing for isn't here yet, and the part that is, you can meet.
cells.sheetLine: You're ending things you haven't been told are over.
cells.verb: Deciding what to release and what to keep, then standing behind the call

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door you already closed, and the room has moved on.
cells.act: feed the drive a little at a time
cells.ask: Choose the smallest next piece of something you meant to finish — ten minutes, one page, one call. Do only that today, stop when it's done, and leave the rest for tomorrow.
cells.core:
Things have ended that you haven't let finish in you. You keep some of it running on the inside while none of it moves on the outside, so the light you steer toward has gone dim without anything replacing it. What you want isn't lost — you've stopped taking steps toward it, and the missing steps are small ones, not the big declaration.

You don't need a new direction. You need fuel, a little at a time, on the thing you already chose. One piece today, done and left alone, teaches you more about what you actually want than a month of deciding would. Keep the fire fed, not fed up — just warm enough that tomorrow's piece is possible. The door behind you doesn't have to close for the next one to open.
cells.sheetLine: You know the direction. You've stopped walking it.

cells.tense: You are deciding things already, and telling the story as though somebody else did.
cells.act: cut through the inertia with one decisive act
cells.ask: Pick the thing already settled and act on it once today, in a motion someone could see. Jot a line to yourself that you chose it, then let it go.
cells.core:
You keep what matters and release what doesn't, and you've been doing it while calling it something else — following along, seeing what was needed, the way things happened to fall. Other people feel the order when you do the arranging, even while your own account of yourself leaves you out of the story.

That's what makes the pull toward what you want feel borrowed rather than yours. Steady arrangement is already underway. The account just hasn't caught up. So carry out a decision you've made where it can be seen, and put your name on it — not a speech, just the plain fact of choosing. The work gets done either way. Right now it's the only thing about it that doesn't know it's yours.
cells.sheetLine: You're arranging it already. Only your story left you out.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim: I cannot know that the person composts endings into new ground, only that the capacity to release-and-keep is operating in this seat today. A reader could reasonably object that they don't steward anyone's material world at all — so every core locates the pattern in a moment of deciding what to keep and what to let go, never in a role. The ask survives being wrong: each is one small visible move that teaches the person something about their own timing whether or not my read holds. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line about 'what the old version is fertilizing' — cut as too flattering, and because it names the mechanism aloud.
